tldr_text:
Loud explosions were heard in Yemen's capital Sanaa on Saturday as Houthis reported Saudi air strikes. Flames and smoke rose from an Aramco facility south of Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh. Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV reported "Saudi aggression" and missile strikes on the telecommunications ministry. Saudi Arabia plans a military offensive against the Houthis in Yemen.

Russia struck Kyiv's Northern Bridge early Saturday, damaging the road surface and trolleybus cables, suspending traffic. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed this second major bridge hit in recent days. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed responsibility, stating the bridge facilitates troop movements and military cargo deliveries for Ukraine. Two people were injured.

Brazil's first round of voting takes place October 4, with President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva facing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. Polls suggest Lula and Bolsonaro are in a virtual tie in a simulated run-off. Wall Street prepares for different market predictions based on the outcome, while Jacobin cites alleged US intervention.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a review of UK-Europe relationship options, including rejoining the European Union. A megapoll by the Messina Group found almost half of voters support Burnham's preference. Renegotiating the relationship could boost Labour's vote share by seven points if a fresh referendum is offered.

The Ebola death toll in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 4,000. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot announced increased French funding and support during a visit to Bunia. France previously allocated €13.4 million, and Barrot plans additional humanitarian funding.

A Flydubai co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe, attempting to take control of the aircraft. United Arab Emirates authorities described the Wednesday, September 30 incident as a terrorist attack. Passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, after the plane plunged 17,000 feet.

Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan, two Iranian men, were charged with preparing terrorist acts. Prosecutors allege contact with an overseas third party, likely an Iranian national, regarding a plot targeting Manchester's Jewish community, including the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park Synagogue.

Pakistan summoned India's Chargé d'Affaires to protest the killing of two Pakistani civilians by Indian Border Security Force personnel in the Bedian Sector along the International Border near Kasur on October 2. Pakistan's Foreign Office stated BSF personnel used "unprovoked lethal force" against unarmed civilians.

President Donald Trump announced a one-time $90 payment to over 20 million Medicare enrollees. Funds will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, with most recipients expecting direct deposits in early October.

Joshua Kerry, 28, faces charges for preparing terrorist acts, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. The alleged acts occurred between May 2024 and July 2026. Kerry was previously charged with the murder of former lawmaker Ann Widdecombe, who died July 9, 2026.

## OPEN
A: From Void News, this is On Air. It's Saturday, October third. French student protests have escalated, leading to thousands of arrests.

## MENU
A: On the desk today.
A: French student protests lead to widespread disruption and violence.
B: Ebola deaths in Congo surpass four thousand amid drug trials.
A: President Trump announces payments for Medicare seniors.
B: Brazil's presidential election first round is tomorrow.
A: Two Iranian men face terror charges in Manchester.

## STORY 1 | French Student Protests
A: French student unions call for new rallies on October sixth. This follows talks with Education Minister Édouard Geffray on Friday. The talks did not yield immediate concrete commitments. Louis Letoublon, vice-president of Les Lycéens, expressed disappointment after the meeting. He says no specific measures were received.
A: Police have arrested more than five thousand people since the protests began. Most of those arrested are minors. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported one thousand seven hundred forty-seven arrests on Friday alone. Édouard Geffray stated one hundred seventy students and sixty-five school staff members have been injured. Forty head teachers are among the injured staff.
A: Over three hundred police officers also sustained injuries. More than one hundred secondary schools suffered severe damage. Fires were reported in some locations. P-J Media attributes the escalation of violence to outside agitators. They cite a French cabinet crisis meeting readout. The readout describes the movement as an operation organized by L-F-I and its proxies on the far left. Other sources describe the violence as an escalation of student frustrations.
B: Time reports roughly three thousand arrests since the protests began, with nearly two thousand detained on Thursday alone.

## STORY 2 | Congo Ebola Outbreak
B: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Ebola death toll has surpassed four thousand. An experimental drug trial for a post-exposure prophylaxis targeting the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola is underway. This trial is happening in eastern Ituri Province. The Ebola outbreak was officially declared in mid-May. It has since spread to seven provinces. Ituri is identified as the epicenter.
B: France will increase its funding and support to combat Ebola. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot announced this on October third. He made the announcement during a visit to Bunia. France previously allocated almost fourteen million euros to the Ebola fight. This funding was provided between January and July.
B: Minister Barrot plans to propose additional humanitarian funding. This will occur during upcoming French budget discussions. A national humanitarian conference in Paris on October sixth will address Ebola. Authorities report at least eight thousand three hundred confirmed cases. They also report four thousand deaths since mid-May.
A: C-G-T-N reports that the Ebola outbreak is easing in the D-R Congo, but the Africa C-D-C warns against this interpretation.

## STORY 3 | Trump Medicare Payments
A: President Donald Trump announced late Friday that his administration will send a one-time payment. The payment is ninety dollars. It goes to more than twenty million Americans enrolled in Medicare. The payments are intended to help offset monthly insurance premium costs.
A: The total payments will be approximately two billion dollars. These funds will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund. Most eligible Medicare Part B enrollees expect to receive the funds via direct deposit. This is expected in early October. Others will receive a mailed check.
A: Sources differ on the exact amount of the payment. Some state nearly one hundred dollars. Others specify ninety dollars. Some sources highlight President Trump's characterization of the Medicare Improvement Fund. He called it a slush fund. Other sources focus on the payment's purpose and recipient numbers.
B: The payments are expected to reach recipients in early October.

## STORY 4 | Brazil Election
B: Voting is from eight in the morning to five in the afternoon Brasilia time. Brazilian voters face a choice between left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. Flavio Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
B: Polls suggest Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are in a virtual tie in a simulated run-off. Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term. Wall Street is preparing for starkly different market predictions. These predictions depend on the election outcome.
B: Fernando Marengo, chief economist at Black Toro Global Investments, stated the Brazil trade is, in his words, Does Lula win or does Bolsonaro win? C-N-B-C focuses on the economic implications of the election. Al Jazeera and The Guardian provide more general overviews of the candidates. Jacobin and i News emphasize alleged U-S intervention in the election.
A: Jacobin cites Brazil's national intelligence agency, A-B-I-N, regarding alleged U-S intervention.

## FINALLY | 19 | WNBA Semifinals
B: One more before Void Opinion. The Golden State Valkyries advanced to the W-N-B-A semifinals on Friday night. They defeated the Dallas Wings seventy-seven to seventy-three in a deciding Game Three of their first-round playoff series. The Valkyries, in their second season, clinched their first-ever playoff series on home court. During the game, with less than two minutes remaining, Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase collapsed on the sideline. Athletic trainer Katelin Knox quickly came to her side. Nakase was helped up and returned to the bench to lead the team's huddle. E-S-P-N’s Kendra Andrews reports Nakase was feeling exhausted and lightheaded but was fine after the game.

opinion_text:
More than 5,000 people, mostly minors, have been arrested across France since student protests over education conditions began. On Friday alone, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported 1,747 arrests. These detentions follow talks between student unions and Education Minister Édouard Geffray that yielded no immediate concrete commitments. Louis Letoublon, vice-president of Les Lycéens, expressed disappointment after the meeting, stating no specific measures were received.

The human cost of this unrest is clear. Édouard Geffray stated 170 students and 65 school staff members, including 40 head teachers, have been injured. Over 300 police officers also sustained injuries. The physical infrastructure of public education has suffered too. More than 100 secondary schools sustained severe damage, and fires were reported at schools, including one in Metz. On Friday, protests affected 735 of France's 3,700 schools.

Students demand improvements to dilapidated facilities, teacher shortages, and overcrowded classrooms. These are not new grievances. They are systemic failures that have festered, creating an environment where frustration boils over. The government has condemned the violence, yet its response has prioritized control and repression over addressing the root causes of student anger. We see a pattern where the state meets calls for investment in public services with a show of force.

The narrative of "outside agitators" or "professional radical left activists" deflects from the lived reality of students. It ignores the fundamental issues that drive thousands of young people into the streets. When public institutions fail to provide a basic standard of education, when dialogue yields no concrete commitments, and when the primary response is mass arrests of minors, the state itself creates the conditions for escalation. We must ask who bears the cost of this neglect. It is the students, their families, and the future of public education.

The cycle of protest, injury, and arrest will continue until the government moves beyond condemnation and offers tangible solutions to the very real problems students face. The current approach only deepens the chasm between the state and its youth. We stand at a point where the damage to schools is mirrored by the damage to trust in public institutions.
